steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
WSI and computational pathology
- whole slide image (WSI) scanning revolutionized computational pathology research
- easy access to WSIs for researchers and clinicians
- but processing and storing gigapixel images still challenging

Motivation
- two main challenges: large image size; scarce or missing patch-level labels (annotations)
- most SOTA methods: Multi-instance Learning (MIL), weak supervision
- MIL removes need for pixel-level annotations, but raises computational load, possibly lower quality than fully supervised
- attempts to select representative patches; many still computationally intensive -> efficient, accurate solutions still unmet need

Models from natural images
- digital pathology mostly adopts deep models designed for natural images, not customized
- pre-trained models may not exploit unique traits of histopathology images
- training recipes for histopathological embeddings: conventional training + common natural-image augmentations
- histopathology images very different from natural and even radiology images -> motivates improved training approach

Contributions (prose)
- two-fold: selective patching + robust feature extraction
- fast patch selection FPS: "divide & conquer", compact yet highly representative subset of patches; tuned to balance computational efficiency and diagnostic utility
- PathDino: lightweight histopathology-specific transformer, five small vision transformer blocks; superior performance, less overfitting
- HistoRotate: seamless 360^{\circ} rotation augmentation for training histopathology models; combined with PathDino -> better embeddings, less overfitting
- validated on multiple datasets: computational efficiency + superior performance

Contribution list
- Fast Patch Selection: compact, spatially diverse patch subset from WSI; lower computational overhead, representational fidelity kept
- PathDino: 5 transformer blocks, 9 million parameters, less overfitting
- Rotation-Agnostic Representation Training: HistoRotate, 360^{\circ} rotation; rotating histopathological patches keeps general context, unlike natural images
- Extensive Evaluation: eleven datasets, competitive to superior vs. SOTA

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Whole slide image (WSI) scanning has changed research in computational pathology a lot. Digital pathology lets both researchers and clinicians get easy access to the WSIs, but these images are gigapixel images and processing and storing them is still quite challenging.

Motivation: There are two main challenges in WSI analysis, the large image size and the fact that patch-level labels (annotations) are scarce or missing. Because of this, most state-of-the-art methods use Multi-instance Learning (MIL) with weak supervision. These approaches may remove the need for pixel-level annotations, but MIL increases the computational load a lot and it can lower the quality of the results compared to fully supervised approaches. Some attempts have been made to select representative patches, but many of these methods are still computationally intensive, so efficient and accurate solutions are still an unmet need.

For image analysis in digital pathology, the field has mostly used deep models that were designed for natural images, without customizing them for the field. Pre-trained deep models perform well on natural images, but they may not fully exploit the unique characteristics of histopathology images. Also, most current training recipes for learning histopathological embeddings use conventional training and the common augmentation techniques for natural images. But histopathology images have quite different features compared to natural images and even compared to radiology images. This gap is what motivated us to design a better training approach for histopathology images.

Contributions (prose)
- two-fold: selective patching + robust feature extraction
- fast patch selection FPS: "divide & conquer", compact yet highly representative subset of patches; tuned to balance computational efficiency and diagnostic utility
- PathDino: lightweight histopathology-specific transformer, five small vision transformer blocks; superior performance, less overfitting
- HistoRotate: seamless 360^{\circ} rotation augmentation for training histopathology models; combined with PathDino -> better embeddings, less overfitting
- validated on multiple datasets: computational efficiency + superior performance

Contribution list
- Fast Patch Selection: compact, spatially diverse patch subset from WSI; lower computational overhead, representational fidelity kept
- PathDino: 5 transformer blocks, 9 million parameters, less overfitting
- Rotation-Agnostic Representation Training: HistoRotate, 360^{\circ} rotation; rotating histopathological patches keeps general context, unlike natural images
- Extensive Evaluation: eleven datasets, competitive to superior vs. SOTA

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Whole slide image (WSI) scanning has changed research in computational pathology a lot. Digital pathology lets both researchers and clinicians get easy access to the WSIs, but these images are gigapixel images and processing and storing them is still quite challenging.

Motivation: There are two main challenges in WSI analysis, the large image size and the fact that patch-level labels (annotations) are scarce or missing. Because of this, most state-of-the-art methods use Multi-instance Learning (MIL) with weak supervision. These approaches may remove the need for pixel-level annotations, but MIL increases the computational load a lot and it can lower the quality of the results compared to fully supervised approaches. Some attempts have been made to select representative patches, but many of these methods are still computationally intensive, so efficient and accurate solutions are still an unmet need.

For image analysis in digital pathology, the field has mostly used deep models that were designed for natural images, without customizing them for the field. Pre-trained deep models perform well on natural images, but they may not fully exploit the unique characteristics of histopathology images. Also, most current training recipes for learning histopathological embeddings use conventional training and the common augmentation techniques for natural images. But histopathology images have quite different features compared to natural images and even compared to radiology images. This gap is what motivated us to design a better training approach for histopathology images.

Contributions: Our solution has two parts, selective patching and robust feature extraction. First, we propose fast patch selection (FPS), a "divide & conquer" algorithm that can find a compact but highly representative subset of patches for analysis. The algorithm has been carefully tuned to balance computational efficiency and diagnostic utility. Second, we introduce PathDino, which is a lightweight histopathology-specific transformer that has just five small vision transformer blocks, and it is customized and tuned to the nuances of histopathological images. It performs better and it also reduces susceptibility to overfitting. We also propose HistoRotate, a seamless 360^{\circ} rotation augmentation technique designed specifically for training histopathology models. Using this augmentation together with the lightweight histopathology-specific transformer makes the embedding quality significantly better and mitigates overfitting. We validate our model with extensive evaluation on multiple datasets, and it shows both computational efficiency and superior performance. Our key contributions are:

- Fast Patch Selection: A new, efficient patch selection mechanism that picks a compact, spatially diverse subset of patches from the WSI, which reduces computational overhead and keeps representational fidelity.

- PathDino: A lightweight histopathology-specific Vision Transformer with only 5 transformer blocks and 9 million parameters in total, which is less susceptible to overfitting.

- Rotation-Agnostic Representation Training: HistoRotate, a 360^{\circ} rotation augmentation technique for training histopathological image analysis models. Rotating histopathological patches keeps the general context, unlike natural images, and it improves embedding learning.

- Extensive Evaluation: Comprehensive experiments on eleven datasets, with competitive to superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The advent of whole slide image (WSI) scanning in digital pathology has revolutionized research in computational pathology [1,2,3]. While digital pathology gives both researchers and clinicians easy access to WSIs, processing and storing these gigapixel images remains quite challenging.

Motivation: Large image size and scarce or missing patch-level labels (annotations) are the two main challenges in WSI analysis [4]. As a result, most state-of-the-art methods adopt Multi-instance Learning (MIL) with weak supervision [5,6,7,8,9,10,11,12,13]. While these approaches may eliminate the need for pixel-level annotations, MIL significantly increases computational loads and can lower the quality of results compared to fully supervised approaches. Some attempts have been made to select representative patches [14,5,6,15], but many such methods remain computationally intensive, leaving efficient, accurate solutions an unmet need.

The field of image analysis in digital pathology has mostly adopted deep models designed for natural image analysis without further customization [16,17,18,19]. While they perform well on natural images, pre-trained deep models may not fully exploit the unique characteristics of histopathology images. Furthermore, most current training recipes for histopathological embedding learning use conventional training and common augmentation techniques for natural images [18]. However, histopathology images have very different features compared to natural images and even radiology images. This gap motivated us to design an improved training approach for histopathology images.

Contributions: We present a two-fold solution that covers selective patching and robust feature extraction. First, we propose a fast patch selection (FPS), a "divide & conquer" algorithm capable of identifying a compact yet highly representative subset of patches for analysis. This algorithm has been carefully tuned to balance computational efficiency and diagnostic utility. Second, we introduce PathDino, a lightweight histopathology-specific transformer consisting of just five small vision transformer blocks, customized and finely tuned to the nuances of histopathological images. It exhibits superior performance and also reduces susceptibility to overfitting. We also propose HistoRotate, a seamless 360^{\circ} rotation augmentation technique designed specifically for training histopathology models. Combining this augmentation technique with the proposed lightweight transformer significantly enhances embedding quality and mitigates overfitting. Our model is validated through extensive evaluation on multiple datasets, showing both computational efficiency and superior performance. Overall, our key contributions are as follows:

- Fast Patch Selection: A novel and efficient patch selection mechanism that curates a compact, spatially diverse subset of patches from a WSI, reducing computational overhead while maintaining representational fidelity.

- PathDino: A lightweight histopathology-specific Vision Transformer with only 5 transformer blocks, totaling 9 million parameters, with reduced susceptibility to overfitting.

- Rotation-Agnostic Representation Training: We propose HistoRotate, a 360^{\circ} rotation augmentation technique for training histopathological image analysis models. Unlike with natural images, rotating histopathological patches maintains the general context while enhancing embedding learning.

- Extensive Evaluation: Comprehensive experiments across eleven datasets, demonstrating competitive to superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.
